title: A private chef company built around the details of service
intro: Choosing a private chef company in Dubai means choosing how your enquiry, menu, staffing and service will be coordinated. myCHEF connects clients with independent chefs and authorised culinary partners according to the work a booking needs. The useful question is how that arrangement will function for you: who helps shape the brief, what is confirmed before the date and where you go when something changes. This guide brings those practical details into view so you can understand the service behind the name and the experience you are considering.

sections.title: One brief, with the right people for the work
paragraphs: A household visit may need a single chef and a straightforward schedule. An occasion may also need an assistant, hospitality professionals, equipment and coordination. The proposed team should follow the scope, with each role confirmed rather than inferred from a general description of the business.

Tell us the result you want and the support you expect. We can discuss a workable format and the details that need to be agreed. The relationship begins with a clear proposal and continues through practical communication, whether you are booking one dinner or developing a regular cooking routine.

sections.title: Send a brief that makes the first proposal useful
paragraphs: A useful enquiry can be short and still contain the essentials. Include your Dubai location, preferred date or start date, number of people, the meals you need and any essential dietary requirements. Add whether the service is a recurring household arrangement or a one-off occasion, because those lead to different menus, staffing and pricing discussions.

Then describe what a successful result would feel like. Perhaps you want dinner ready when you arrive home, a fridge organised for several busy days or a celebration where you can stay with your guests. This helps the team recommend a suitable format instead of making you choose from options that do not address your main priority.

If you have a budget in mind, share it with the scope. That creates a practical starting point for discussing the number of courses, frequency or staffing. An enquiry begins a conversation; the final menu, availability, responsibilities and price are confirmed in the written booking details.

sections.title: Give every person in the service a clear role
paragraphs: Cooking, carrying plates, pouring drinks and clearing a table are different jobs. For a quiet household visit, you may need only a chef. For an occasion with several courses or guests arriving together, an assistant or service professional can help the kitchen and dining area run at the right pace. Staffing should follow the work, rather than a fixed assumption based only on headcount.

Discuss who will greet guests, replenish water, serve each course and clear used plates. If the chef is expected to do all of those tasks while cooking, the menu and timing need to allow for it. Extra support can be especially useful when the kitchen is far from the dining table or the meal involves several dietary variations.

Your proposal should identify the included roles and service hours. Additional hospitality, equipment and event coordination should be agreed as part of the scope. That clarity lets everyone focus on their responsibilities and gives you a more relaxed experience as host.

sections.title: Look for a chef whose strengths fit the brief
paragraphs: A chef who excels at an elaborate tasting menu may not be the best match for a household that wants simple daily meals and careful batch preparation. Start with the work you actually need: particular cuisines, family cooking, confident service for guests or a regular routine with multiple meals. Relevant experience matters more than a list of impressive-sounding dishes.

Discuss the proposed chef's approach to your kitchen and schedule. How would the menu fit the available hours? Which dishes work well for later meals? What information would they need before the first visit? These practical questions make an introduction more useful than a general conversation about favourite food.

myCHEF considers the brief alongside availability when recommending a match. Profiles can help you understand cooking interests and service styles, but the proposed arrangement still needs confirmation. If you would like a paid trial or tasting, agree the purpose, menu and price first so you know exactly what you will be assessing.

sections.title: Set expectations for discretion in your home
paragraphs: Inviting a chef into your home involves more than sharing a kitchen. Explain any household boundaries before the visit: rooms that are private, preferred routes through the property and how to communicate while you are working or entertaining. Practical instructions make it easier for the service to fit naturally into your day.

Photography should be discussed separately from cooking. If your household does not want photographs taken, say so clearly in the brief. Any request to share images of a booking should be handled with the relevant permission; a meal at home is not automatically a marketing opportunity. You can also raise any specific confidentiality requirements before confirming the arrangement.

Keep sensitive details proportionate to what is needed for the service. Menus, allergies and arrival instructions help the chef do the job; unrelated personal information usually does not. Your myCHEF contact can help clarify how a privacy request affects the booking and which details need to be passed to the proposed professional.

sections.title: Look beyond the finished table when reviewing previous work
paragraphs: The finished setting is only one part of an occasion. When reviewing a previous service, look at how the food was presented, how guests could reach it and how the setup suited the venue. A compact yacht table, a villa dining room and a larger reception each call for different decisions, even when the overall style feels similar.

Use documented examples to ask practical questions about your own brief. Would the same format work with your guest count? Does your venue have comparable preparation space? Would additional staff be needed to serve the dishes in the way you want? These questions turn a portfolio into a useful planning tool rather than a collection of attractive images.

A previous booking is not a fixed package or a promise of identical availability. Menus, seasonal ingredients, staffing and equipment need to be reviewed for each occasion. Share the elements you like, and the team can explain how a suitable version could be planned around your date, property and expectations.

sections.title: Judge the service by the difference it makes at home
paragraphs: The value of a private chef is not measured only by the number of dishes prepared. Consider whether the meals are being enjoyed, whether the timing works and whether the arrangement reduces the decisions you need to make each day. A reliable favourite served when you need it can be more useful than an ambitious menu that does not fit your routine.

Review the service against the priorities in your original brief. Are the portions right? Is shopping clear? Do you understand what is ready for later? Are the booked hours being used for the tasks you care about most? These questions help you identify a practical adjustment before deciding that the whole arrangement needs to change.

For an occasion, think about your experience as host as well as the food. Clear coordination, suitable staffing and a manageable service format can give you more time with guests. The best proposal is the one that connects its price and scope to the experience you actually want.
